newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council calls for ceasefire in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council calls for ceasefire in Zaire.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council on Friday demanded a ceasefire in eastern Zaire and called on the international community to come up with an urgent response to the crisis.

But the council, in a statement read out at a formal meeting, did not suggest any new or dramatic action to stop the fighting between Zairean troops and Tutsi rebel forces that has displaced more than half a million refugees and threatens to inflame the region.
It said there was an "urgent need for a comprehensive and coordinated response by the international community to prevent any further escalation of the crisis."
The statement was read by Council President Nugroho Wisnumurti of Indonesia.

So far all sides have ignored calls for a ceasefire. Zaire's ragged army and allied Rwandan Hutu fighters were facing a humiliating defeat by well-armed rebels in the eastern provinces facing Rwanda and Burundi.
On Friday Rwandan troops were reported by diplomats to have entered the eastern Zaire town of Goma to assist Tutsi rebels but the government denied it.
The council also indicated its concern Zaire would crumble as a state, saying that all nations should respect "the sovereignty and territorial integrity" of their neighbours.

It called for an international conference on the crisis but Zaire's U.N. representative, Lubaku Khabouji N'Zaji, told reporters his country would not attend as long as Rwandan troops were on his territory.
He did not distinguish between regular Rwandan commandos and Zairean Tutsis who have been in the country for centuries.
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali has sent a mission to Zaire, seconding Canada's ambassador to Washington, Raymond Chretien, to see if a ceasefire could be arranged.

But he has not recommended any military intervention in Zaire, realising it would be nearly impossible to get any volunteers. Europeans want African forces to go to the area but there is no sign this is feasible.

In a Thursday report on neighbouring Burundi, Boutros-Ghali said 10,000 people had died in the country's civil war since the Tutsi army staged a military coup on July 25. He said he would continue contingency planning for an international standby force "although there does not yet seem to be sufficient political will for resolute preventive action."

Frustration is increasing among various nations as the crisis escalates. Razali Ismail of Malaysia, the president of the General Assembly said, he had reached the "horrible conclusion that we are unable collectively or individually to do enough to prevent the human tragedies before us."

"We as officeholders and those in positions of responsibility in the United Nations, feel impotent that we are not able to prevent such huge loss of life, despite being able to craft words and resolutions in a beautiful fashion," he said in a statement.

The conflict began with a Zairean army campaign against ethnic Tutsis but springs from the deadly rivalry between Tutsis and Hutus which resulted in nearly one million dead in Rwanda's 1994 genocide and left Zaire the unhappy host to 1.1 million Hutu Rwandan refugees.

The Kinshasa government accuses Rwanda and Burundi, whose armies and governments are dominated by Tutsis, of backing local Tutsis against the Zairean army. Aid workers are unable to get food into large camps in Eastern Zaire.
